topic: wintering two hives: stores, mite load, insulation above the crown board and a split floor

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-1)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem

base: I keep two hives in the orchard and I want the stronger one to winter without feeding.
The weaker colony beside the hedge came through last winter, though it built up very late.
A recording hive scale sits under the weaker stand and logs its weight every hour.
The strong hive has eight frames of sealed stores and a brood nest still spreading downward.
Should I feed syrup now, or first measure what the bees are actually holding?
Weigh the hive first, because frame counts mislead badly once the combs are partly filled.
Lift the back of the strong floor with a spring balance and double the reading you get.
A colony of that size wants roughly eighteen kilograms of stores to reach the willow flow.
Feeding after the middle of October rarely helps, since the bees cannot ripen thin syrup.
I weighed both hives and the strong one holds about twenty kilograms above the empty weight.
The weaker colony beside the hedge came in at barely eleven, which worries me now.
Both hives showed mites on the board, roughly four a day under the strong one.
Do I treat first and feed afterwards, or does the order not matter at this point?
Treat first, because mites damage the very bees that must live through the whole winter.
Winter bees are raised in September, so a heavy mite load then costs you the spring.
Four mites a day on the board suggests a population worth reducing without any delay.
Feed the weaker colony straight afterwards, since eleven kilograms will not carry it to March.
I treated both hives and the drop on the boards has fallen to almost nothing.
The weaker colony took four litres of syrup within a week and has capped most of it.
Now I am wondering about the roofs, because both hives ran damp along the walls.
The hive scale shows the weight climbing steadily since the syrup went on last week.
Should I insulate above the crown board, or open the entrance wider for more air?
Insulate above and leave the entrance as it is, because damp comes from cold ceilings.
Warm moist air rises, meets a cold roof and rains straight back onto the cluster.
A slab of insulation above the crown board keeps that surface warmer than the walls.
Widening the entrance instead chills the cluster and invites mice through the whole winter.
I fitted insulation above both crown boards and the walls are noticeably drier already.
I also pushed mouse guards into both entrances after finding droppings under the orchard hive.
The weaker colony still flies on mild days, while the strong one stays completely shut.
Does that difference mean anything, or is it simply a matter of colony temperament?
A colony that flies on mild days is usually burning stores it cannot easily replace.
The tighter cluster keeps its warmth and eats far less through the darkest weeks.
Restlessness sometimes points to a failing queen, but more often to a thin drafty floor.
Check the floor for gaps before you blame anything happening inside the box itself.
The floor of the weaker hive had a split board letting daylight through one corner.
I slid a spare floor underneath on a still afternoon without opening the brood box.
The bees settled within an hour and the flying on mild days has clearly reduced.
Is there anything left to do before spring, or should I now leave them alone?
Leave them alone now, apart from lifting the back of each hive every few weeks.
That single check tells you whether stores are dropping faster than the season allows.
Clear snow from the entrances after heavy falls, but never knock on the walls.
In February give each colony a block of candy and then let the willow arrive.
